In summary, our research is concerned with

(1) The composition of Paleozoic volcanic rocks and their relation to the tectonic environment of the time and place of their formation, (2) The relation of these volcanic rocks to the tectonics of the western United States, (3) The nature of the crust in the region, (4) The nature of crustal accretion and continental growth in the western United States.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the western part of the continent was formed in the Mesozoic.
the continental growth in western North America has occurred mainly in Mesozoic time.
the continental margin was formed in late Paleozoico–early Mesozoico time by accretion and segregation of sialic material from the mantle and that continental growth has been westward.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the continental growth in the western U.S. was not a continuous, steady-state process but was episodic and punctuated by major tectonic events.
continental crust was formed by the accretion of island arc and oceanic island arc crustal segments to the continental margin.

the continental crust of Nevada and the adjoining area grew in the Paleozoic and early Mesozoic, and the present crust is a composite of the original continental crust and new crust formed in the Mesozoic.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the continental margin of western Nevada was a complex and dynamic system in which volcanic rocks erupted in response to a variety of tectonic settings and that the continental margin evolved through time in a way that was controlled by the relative positions of the continental margin, island-arc systems, and the Pacific Ocean.
there was a major continental growth event that occurred during the Paleozoic, which was followed by the Mesozoic accretion of island arc material to the west coast of North America.
continental growth is not just a function of accretion, but also of the segregation of sialic material along the margin.
